```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", out.width = "85%")
find_proj_root <- function(path = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(path)
  repeat {
    if (length(list.files(path, pattern = "\\.Rproj$"))) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(path)
    if (parent == path) stop("No .Rproj file found above ", getwd())
    path <- parent
  }
}
proj_root <- find_proj_root()
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = proj_root)

# Caching: the slow chunks (marked cache = TRUE) are saved after the first knit and re-used on
# later knits. A cached chunk re-runs if its own code changes, or if its "cache.extra" fingerprint
# changes. We set that fingerprint from the input files here, and later (tune-helper, cv-table) from
# the objects the cached chunks use, so a change anywhere upstream forces a re-run.
file_md5 <- tools::md5sum(file.path(proj_root, c("data/processed/rq1_model_data.rds", "R/utils_models.R")))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache.extra = file_md5)
```

```{r load}
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "utils_data.R"))
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "utils_models.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(knitr)
  library(glmnet)      # ridge / lasso / elastic net
  library(mgcv)        # generalised additive models (smoothing splines)
  library(rpart)       # regression tree
  library(rpart.plot)  # drawing the tree
  library(ranger)      # random forest (fast, multi-core)
  library(xgboost)     # gradient-boosted trees
  library(e1071)       # support vector machine
})
N_CORES <- max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1)   # leave one core free for the computer
dir.create(paths$models_rq1, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

rq1 <- readRDS(file.path(paths$processed, "rq1_model_data.rds"))

dat <- rq1 |>
  filter(year >= 1996,                                                   # EDA decision 7
         !ta %in% c("Chatham Islands Territory", "Kawerau District")) |>  # too few rows, see 2.3
  droplevels()

train <- dat |> filter(split == "train")   # 1996Q1–2019Q4
test  <- dat |> filter(split == "test")    # 2020Q1–2026Q2: NOT touched until section 13
c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test), districts = nlevels(dat$ta))
```

# Purpose and plan

Steps 1 and 2 gave us a clean table and a list of decisions. Step 3 fits models to it. We go **from the simplest
model to the most flexible**. A complex model has to *earn* its place by beating the simpler ones on data it has
not seen.

| Order | Model | What it can capture | Settings tuned (hyperparameters) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Baselines: overall mean, district mean | Nothing / "each place has its own level" | none |
| 1 | Linear regression (OLS) | Straight-line effects, added up | none |
| 2 | Polynomial regression | Curved effects of each feature | degree |
| 3 | Ridge, lasso, elastic net | Straight lines, with shrinkage / feature selection | penalty λ (α fixed per model) |
| 4 | GAM (smoothing splines) | Any smooth curve per feature | smoothness (chosen automatically by REML) |
| 5 | Regression tree | Thresholds and interactions, as one tree | complexity `cp`, `minbucket` |
| 6 | Random forest | Many de-correlated trees, averaged | `mtry`, `min.node.size` |
| 7 | XGBoost (boosted trees) | Trees added one by one, each fixing the last one's errors | `max_depth`, `min_child_weight`, number of rounds |
| 8 | Support vector machine (radial) | Smooth non-linear surface in all features at once | `cost`, `gamma` |

The pitch named linear, lasso, regression tree and random forest. The others were added because they cover gaps:
polynomial and GAM test whether the effects are curved, XGBoost is the usual strongest method on tables like
ours, and the SVM is a different, distance-based kind of model.

**Ground rules**

1. **Tuning happens on the training years only**, by time-ordered cross-validation (section 4).
2. **The test years (2020–2026) are used once**, at the end (section 13), for every model at its tuned settings.
   We do not go back and change anything after seeing the test scores.
3. **The model is chosen on the cross-validation score**, not the test score. Picking by test score would make the
   test score optimistic.

# What goes into the models

## Response (the label)

The main response is **`rel_log_cost_m2`**: the log of a district's real $/m² *minus* the log of the real
$/m² of all the *other* districts in the same quarter (Step 1, `relative` chunk). Step 2 showed why:

* time explains about 41% of the variation in log real $/m², and the district only about 19%. A model of raw cost
  would mostly learn "which year is it?";
* the relative response removes the national level each quarter, which leaves the "across districts"
  part of RQ1;
* the shift from training to test is small for the relative response (mean −0.04 → −0.01), but large for raw
  cost (+17%). So patterns learned before 2020 should still hold afterwards.

A value of +0.10 means "about 10% dearer than the rest of NZ in that quarter" (strictly e^0.10^ − 1 = 10.5%).

The **secondary response** `log_real_cost_m2` (the pitch's original target) is modelled in section 15. It is mainly
there to show what happens when trees have to predict a price level they never saw.

## Features (the predictors)

```{r features}
Y <- "rel_log_cost_m2"

# numeric drivers (Step 1 built them; Step 2 kept them)
num_main <- c("rel_house_m2",        # house size relative to other districts (log ratio)
              "log_houses_n",        # how many new houses (log)
              "multiunit_share",     # share of new dwellings that are not stand-alone houses
              "apt_share",           # share that are apartments
              "retire_share",        # share that are retirement-village units
              "dwell_per_1000",      # new dwellings per 1000 residents (12 months)
              "houses_yoy",          # growth in house numbers vs the same quarter last year (log)
              "log_resid_alt_real",  # real $ of residential alterations (log)
              "log_nonres_real")     # real $ of new non-residential building (log)

# two feature sets
fsets <- list(
  drivers  = c(num_main, "region", "is_city"),  # measurable drivers + broad location
  district = c(num_main, "ta")                  # measurable drivers + the district itself
)

tibble(feature = c(num_main, "region", "is_city", "ta"),
       type    = map_chr(feature, \(v) class(train[[v]])[1]),
       `in drivers set`  = feature %in% fsets$drivers,
       `in district set` = feature %in% fsets$district) |>
  kable(caption = "Features in each set")
```

**Why two feature sets?** RQ1 asks *what drives* cost. The district name is not a driver: it is a label that soaks
up everything about a place that our measured features miss (land, terrain, local builders, consent rules).

* The **drivers** set leaves the district name out. Whatever it explains has to come from measurable things.
* The **district** set adds the name. The gap between the two sets shows how much of the location effect our
  features *don't* explain.

`region` and `is_city` are left out of the district set because the district already determines them. In a linear
model they would be perfectly collinear and their coefficients could not be estimated.

**Left out on purpose**

* anything built from house *value* (leakage, Step 1);
* lagged cost (a forecasting question, not an explanatory one; Step 2 decision 8);
* island and season (no signal, Step 2 decision 3);
* the time index (the relative response has no trend to follow);
* `avg_house_m2`, which is replaced by `rel_house_m2` for the relative response (Step 2 decision 5).

## Rows

```{r rows}
rq1 |> filter(year >= 1996) |>
  filter(ta %in% c("Chatham Islands Territory", "Kawerau District")) |>
  count(ta, split) |> kable(caption = "Rows dropped (1996 onwards)")
colSums(is.na(train[c(num_main, "rel_log_cost_m2")]))   # expect all zero
```

**Observation.** From 1996 every feature is present, so nothing needs imputing. We drop **Chatham Islands** and
**Kawerau**, which have only 1–2 modelled rows each. A district effect can't be learned from one row, and their
names would appear in the test data but in no training fold (R stops with *"factor has new levels"*).

# Compute check: will this fit on a laptop?

```{r compute}
design_district <- make_x(train, paste(fsets$district, collapse = " + "))
tibble(object = c("all modelled rows (rq1)", "training rows", "design matrix, district set"),
       rows   = c(nrow(rq1), nrow(train), nrow(design_district)),
       columns = c(ncol(rq1), ncol(train), ncol(design_district)),
       MB     = c(object.size(rq1), object.size(train), object.size(design_district)) / 2^20) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
ram_gb <- tryCatch(as.numeric(system("sysctl -n hw.memsize", intern = TRUE)) / 2^30,   # macOS only
                   error = function(e) NA, warning = function(e) NA)
c(cores_available = parallel::detectCores(), cores_used = N_CORES, RAM_GB = ram_gb)
```

**Observation.** The data takes a few megabytes. The machine has gigabytes. Memory is not a constraint. The
heaviest object will be a 500-tree random forest (tens of MB). The real cost is *time*: every tuning setting is
fitted four times (one per fold). That's why the slow chunks are cached, and why `ranger` and `xgboost` use several
cores.

# How models are compared fairly

## Metrics

All errors are on the **log scale**, where an error of 0.10 ≈ 10% of $/m².

* **RMSE** (root mean squared error): penalises big misses. It is the main score.
* **MAE** (mean absolute error): the typical miss.
* **R²**: share of the variation explained. 0 = no better than predicting the average; 1 = perfect.
* **MAPE** on $/m² (test only): the pitch's metric. Predicted $/m² = e^prediction^ × (the other districts'
  $/m² that quarter).

## Time-ordered cross-validation

Tuning needs a score for each candidate setting, computed on data the model did not train on. We can't use the test
set for this (ground rule 2). Ordinary random k-fold CV would mix 2018 rows into training when validating on 2014,
which lets the model see the future. We use **forward-chaining** folds instead: train on every year before a block,
validate on the block.

```{r folds, fig.height = 2.6}
folds <- make_time_folds(train$year)

fold_plot <- imap_dfr(folds, \(f, nm) bind_rows(
  tibble(fold = nm, year = unique(train$year[f$train]), role = "train"),
  tibble(fold = nm, year = unique(train$year[f$valid]), role = "validate")))

p_folds <- ggplot(fold_plot, aes(year, fct_rev(fold), fill = role)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", height = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(train = "#9ecae1", validate = "#e6550d")) +
  labs(title = "Forward-chaining cross-validation folds (training years only)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL)
save_fig(p_folds, "fig15_cv_folds", height = 2.6)

sapply(folds, \(f) c(train_rows = length(f$train), valid_rows = length(f$valid)))
```

**Observation.** There are four folds, each validating on two years (about 470 rows) after training on 3,800–5,200
rows. The last fold (train 1996–2017, validate 2018–19) is closest to the real task. The **CV score** of a setting
is its average RMSE over the four folds. Its spread across folds gives a standard error.

## How tuning works, and the one-standard-error rule

For each model, `cv_tune()` (in `R/utils_models.R`) does the following:

1. for every row of a grid of settings and every fold, fit on the fold's training rows and predict its validation
   rows;
2. average the validation RMSE over folds;
3. return the setting with the lowest average.

**Choosing between models** uses the **one-standard-error rule**: take the lowest CV RMSE, add one standard error,
and choose the *simplest* model under that line. Differences smaller than the fold-to-fold noise are not worth
the extra complexity or the lost interpretability.

Every model below is written as a small "factory": `fp_x(vars, y)` returns a function that fits on one data set
and predicts another. `tune_model()` runs it on both feature sets.

```{r tune-helper}
rhs_of <- function(vars) paste(vars, collapse = " + ")
fml_of <- function(y, vars) as.formula(paste(y, "~", rhs_of(vars)))
is_num <- function(v) is.numeric(train[[v]])

tune_model <- function(factory, grid = NULL, inner = NULL, sets = fsets, y = Y) {
  imap(sets, \(vars, nm) timed(cv_tune(factory(vars, y), grid, train, folds, y, inner)))
}

# fingerprint of everything the cached tuning chunks depend on (if any of it changes, they re-run)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache.extra = list(file_md5, rlang::hash(list(train, folds, fsets, Y, N_CORES))))
```

# Baselines

**What they are.** The *overall mean* predicts the training average for every row. The *district mean* predicts
each district's own training average (the baseline Step 2 chose). Any useful model must beat the district mean;
otherwise "it's Queenstown, so it's dear" would be all we've learned.

```{r baselines}
fp_mean <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p) rep(mean(tr[[y]]), nrow(nw))

fp_district_mean <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p) {
  m   <- tapply(tr[[y]], tr$ta, mean)        # one average per district
  out <- unname(m[as.character(nw$ta)])
  ifelse(is.na(out), mean(tr[[y]]), out)     # a district never seen gets the overall mean
}

res_mean     <- tune_model(fp_mean,          sets = list(none = character(0)))
res_distmean <- tune_model(fp_district_mean, sets = list(none = character(0)))
bind_rows(summarise_tuning(res_mean, "Overall mean"),
          summarise_tuning(res_distmean, "District mean")) |>
  select(model, cv_rmse, cv_rmse_se, cv_mae, cv_r2) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

**Observation.** The overall mean misses by about `r round(res_mean$none$best$cv_rmse, 3)` on the log scale (≈
`r round(100 * res_mean$none$best$cv_rmse)`%). Knowing only the district cuts this to
`r round(res_distmean$none$best$cv_rmse, 3)` (CV R² = `r round(res_distmean$none$best$cv_r2, 2)`). That is a strong
baseline: Step 2 showed that districts keep their rank for decades. **This is the number to beat.**

# Linear regression (OLS)

**What it is.** *Ordinary least squares*. Prediction = intercept + b₁·x₁ + b₂·x₂ + …. The coefficients b are chosen
to minimise the sum of squared errors. Each coefficient is the change in the response for a one-unit change in that
feature, *holding the others fixed*. There is nothing to tune.

**Assumptions.** Effects are straight lines and add up. Errors have constant spread. For valid p-values, rows must
also be independent. Our rows are not (the same district appears quarter after quarter), so we use OLS for
*prediction and description*, not for formal significance tests.

```{r ols}
fp_ols <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p) predict(lm(fml_of(y, vars), data = tr), newdata = nw)
res_ols <- tune_model(fp_ols)
summarise_tuning(res_ols, "Linear regression") |> select(set, cv_rmse, cv_rmse_se, cv_r2) |> kable(digits = 4)

# coefficients of the drivers model fitted on all training rows (numeric features standardised so sizes compare)
ols_std <- lm(fml_of(Y, fsets$drivers),
              data = train |> mutate(across(all_of(num_main), \(x) as.numeric(scale(x)))))
broom_like <- summary(ols_std)$coefficients
tibble(term = rownames(broom_like), estimate = broom_like[, 1], std_error = broom_like[, 2]) |>
  filter(term %in% num_main | term == "is_cityTRUE") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate))) |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "OLS, drivers set: effect of a 1-SD change in each feature (log points)")
```

**Observation.** OLS on the drivers alone (CV RMSE `r round(res_ols$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)`, R²
`r round(res_ols$drivers$best$cv_r2, 2)`) beats the overall mean, but **not** the district mean. With the district added
(`r round(res_ols$district$best$cv_rmse, 4)`, R² `r round(res_ols$district$best$cv_r2, 2)`) it beats both: the drivers
explain *changes* within a district that the district average can't. In the standardised coefficients, a positive
estimate means "districts with more of this feature are dearer, other features held equal". Alteration spending and
dwellings per 1,000 residents are positive; the number of new houses and relative house size are negative. Because the activity measures overlap (VIF up to ~6 in Step 2),
individual coefficients can swap size or even sign between similar models. Treat them as a description, not a
causal effect.

# Polynomial regression

**What it is.** Still a linear model, but each numeric feature x is also given x², x³, … as extra columns, so its
effect can bend. `poly(x, d)` builds *orthogonal* polynomials, which carry the same information as x, x², … but
are uncorrelated with each other, so the fit is numerically stable. **Tuned:** the degree d (1 = plain OLS).

**Risk.** High-degree polynomials swing wildly beyond the range of the training data. That matters when the test
years bring feature values never seen before.

```{r poly, cache = TRUE}
fp_poly <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p) {
  terms <- map_chr(vars, \(v) if (is_num(v)) sprintf("poly(%s, %d)", v, p$degree) else v)
  predict(lm(as.formula(paste(y, "~", paste(terms, collapse = " + "))), data = tr), newdata = nw)
}
res_poly <- tune_model(fp_poly, grid = tibble(degree = 1:3))
res_poly$drivers$summary |> select(degree, cv_rmse, cv_rmse_sd, cv_r2) |> kable(digits = 4, caption = "Drivers set")
summarise_tuning(res_poly, "Polynomial regression") |> select(set, best_settings, cv_rmse, cv_r2) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

**Observation.** For the drivers set, degree `r res_poly$drivers$best$degree` is best, but only slightly better
than straight lines (`r round(res_poly$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)` vs `r round(res_ols$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)`). For the
district set, degree `r res_poly$district$best$degree` wins, so plain OLS. The relationships bend a little but are
close to linear.

# Ridge, lasso and elastic net (regularised regression)

**What they are.** OLS with a **penalty** on the size of the coefficients:

$$
\min_b \; \sum (y - Xb)^2 / 2n \;+\; \lambda \left[ \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\sum b_j^2 + \alpha \sum |b_j| \right]
$$

* **Ridge** (α = 0) shrinks all coefficients towards zero. It helps when features overlap (our VIFs).
* **Lasso** (α = 1) can shrink coefficients *exactly* to zero, which drops features. That makes it a feature
  selector.
* **Elastic net** (α = 0.5) sits between the two.

**Tuned:** λ, the penalty strength. λ = 0 is plain OLS; a large λ shrinks everything to zero. One `glmnet` fit
gives predictions for a whole sequence of λ values at once, so CV scores 100 λ values almost for free (that's the
"inner" setting in `cv_tune`). `glmnet` standardises the features internally, so the penalty treats them all alike.

```{r glmnet, cache = TRUE}
lambda_grid <- 10^seq(1, -6, length.out = 100)

fp_glmnet <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p) {
  rhs <- rhs_of(vars)
  fit <- glmnet(make_x(tr, rhs), tr[[y]], alpha = p$alpha, lambda = lambda_grid)
  pred <- predict(fit, make_x(nw, rhs))
  colnames(pred) <- fit$lambda
  pred
}
res_ridge <- tune_model(fp_glmnet, grid = tibble(alpha = 0),   inner = "lambda")
res_enet  <- tune_model(fp_glmnet, grid = tibble(alpha = 0.5), inner = "lambda")
res_lasso <- tune_model(fp_glmnet, grid = tibble(alpha = 1),   inner = "lambda")

bind_rows(summarise_tuning(res_ridge, "Ridge"), summarise_tuning(res_enet, "Elastic net"),
          summarise_tuning(res_lasso, "Lasso")) |>
  select(model, set, best_settings, cv_rmse, cv_r2) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

```{r lasso-curve, fig.height = 3.6}
lasso_curve <- imap_dfr(res_lasso, \(r, set) r$summary |> mutate(set = set))
p_lasso <- ggplot(lasso_curve, aes(log10(lambda), cv_rmse, colour = set)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = lasso_curve |> group_by(set) |> slice_min(cv_rmse, n = 1), size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(drivers = "#2a6f97", district = "#e76f51")) +
  labs(title = "Lasso: cross-validated error against penalty strength",
       subtitle = "Right = stronger penalty (fewer features). Dot = best λ.",
       x = expression(log[10](lambda)), y = "CV RMSE (log scale)", colour = "Feature set")
save_fig(p_lasso, "fig16_lasso_cv_curve", height = 3.6)
```

**Observation.** The curve is flat at small λ (≈ OLS), then rises steeply once the penalty starts removing useful
features. Results by feature set:

* **Drivers set** (~25 columns after dummies): the best λ is the smallest one tried, so the penalty does not help at
  all (CV RMSE `r round(res_lasso$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)`, the same as OLS). With 5,000 rows and few columns, OLS is
  not over-fitting.
* **District set** (~74 columns): a small penalty helps a little (`r round(res_ols$district$best$cv_rmse, 4)` →
  `r round(res_lasso$district$best$cv_rmse, 4)`) by pulling the noisy effects of small districts towards the average.
  The gain is well inside one standard error (`r round(res_lasso$district$best$cv_rmse_sd / 2, 4)`).

Ridge, elastic net and lasso end up almost identical, and close to plain OLS.

# Generalised additive model (GAM)

**What it is.** prediction = intercept + f₁(x₁) + f₂(x₂) + …, where each fₖ is a smooth curve (a penalised
regression spline) instead of a straight line or polynomial. It sits between polynomial regression (curves) and
OLS (interpretable, additive).

**Tuned:** how wiggly each curve may be. `mgcv` chooses this itself by **REML**, which balances fit against
smoothness inside a single fit, so there is no grid. `k = 6` caps each curve at 6 basis functions.

```{r gam, cache = TRUE}
fp_gam <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p) {
  terms <- map_chr(vars, \(v) if (is_num(v)) sprintf("s(%s, k = 6)", v) else v)
  fit <- gam(as.formula(paste(y, "~", paste(terms, collapse = " + "))), data = tr, method = "REML")
  as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = nw))
}
res_gam <- tune_model(fp_gam)
summarise_tuning(res_gam, "GAM (splines)") |> select(set, cv_rmse, cv_r2, seconds) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

**Observation.** The GAM does about as well as degree-2 polynomials (`r round(res_gam$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)`),
which confirms that effects bend a little. Smooth curves, one feature at a time, do not close the gap to the
tree ensembles below. That suggests the missing ingredient is *interactions* between features, not curvature.

# Regression tree

**What it is.** The tree repeatedly splits the rows on one feature at a threshold and predicts the average of each
final group. It captures thresholds and interactions and is easy to read, but a single tree is unstable: small
changes in the data can change the splits.

**Tuned:**

* `cp`: the complexity parameter. A split is kept only if it improves fit by at least `cp` × the starting error.
  A small `cp` gives a big tree.
* `minbucket`: the smallest allowed leaf.

`xval = 0` turns off rpart's own random CV because we use our time-ordered folds instead.

```{r tree, cache = TRUE}
fp_tree <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p)
  predict(rpart(fml_of(y, vars), data = tr,
                control = rpart.control(cp = p$cp, minbucket = p$minbucket, xval = 0)), newdata = nw)

res_tree <- tune_model(fp_tree, grid = expand_grid(cp = c(0.0005, 0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02),
                                                   minbucket = c(10, 30, 60)))
summarise_tuning(res_tree, "Regression tree") |> select(set, best_settings, cv_rmse, cv_r2) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

```{r tree-plot, fig.height = 5.5, out.width = "100%"}
best_tree <- res_tree$drivers$best
# short region names so the split labels fit on the page
short_region <- function(r) r |> str_remove(" Region") |>
  str_replace_all(c("Manawatu-Whanganui" = "Manawatu", "Bay of Plenty" = "BoP", "Hawke's Bay" = "HawkesBay",
                    "West Coast" = "WestCoast", "Marlborough" = "Marlb", "Canterbury" = "Canterb",
                    "Northland" = "Northl", "Southland" = "Southl", "Wellington" = "Wgtn"))
train_tree <- train |> mutate(region = fct_relabel(region, short_region))
tree_fit  <- rpart(fml_of(Y, fsets$drivers), data = train_tree,
                   control = rpart.control(cp = max(best_tree$cp, 0.005), minbucket = best_tree$minbucket, xval = 0))
draw_tree <- function() rpart.plot(tree_fit, type = 2, extra = 101, under = TRUE, roundint = FALSE,
                                   box.palette = "BuRd", tweak = 1.0, split.cex = 0.9,
                                   main = "Regression tree, drivers set (pruned for display; red = dearer)")
png(file.path(paths$fig_rq1, "fig17_regression_tree.png"), width = 11, height = 6, units = "in", res = 200)
draw_tree(); invisible(dev.off())
draw_tree()
```

**Observation.** The plotted tree is pruned a bit harder than the tuned one (`cp` ≥ 0.005) so it can be read.
Each box shows the mean relative cost, the number of rows and their share. How to read it:

* The **first split is on residential alteration spending**: districts that spend more on renovations are dearer
  for new houses too.
* Then **region** separates the cheaper provincial regions.
* Then **dwellings per 1,000 residents** (fast-growing places) splits again.
* The dearest leaf (≈ +0.19, about 20% above the rest of NZ, 73 rows) is high-alteration, high-growth
  district-quarters in the regions *not* in the listed group (Auckland, Wellington, Otago, Gisborne, Hawke's Bay,
  West Coast). In practice it is mostly Queenstown-Lakes.

The tuned tree (CV RMSE `r round(res_tree$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)`) is about as accurate as OLS. One tree is too
coarse to beat smoother models, but it shows the drivers *interacting*: the effect of growth depends on the region.

# Random forest

**What it is.** Hundreds of deep trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample of the rows. At each split only a random
subset of `mtry` features may be considered. Averaging many different trees removes most of a single tree's
instability.

**Tuned:**

* `mtry`: features tried at each split. Small values give more varied trees; `mtry` = all features is "bagging".
* `min.node.size`: the smallest leaf. Larger values give smoother predictions.

The number of trees (500) is not really a tuning setting: more trees never hurt, they just take longer, and 500 is
plenty here.

```{r rf, cache = TRUE}
fp_rf <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p)
  predict(ranger(fml_of(y, vars), data = tr, num.trees = 500,
                 mtry = min(p$mtry, length(vars)), min.node.size = p$min.node.size,
                 num.threads = N_CORES, seed = 462), data = nw)$predictions

res_rf <- tune_model(fp_rf, grid = expand_grid(mtry = c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10), min.node.size = c(5, 20, 50)))
summarise_tuning(res_rf, "Random forest") |> select(set, best_settings, cv_rmse, cv_r2, seconds) |> kable(digits = 4)
res_rf$drivers$summary |> select(mtry, min.node.size, cv_rmse) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = min.node.size, values_from = cv_rmse, names_prefix = "min.node.size = ") |>
  arrange(mtry) |> kable(digits = 4, caption = "Drivers set: CV RMSE over the grid")
```

**Observation.** On the drivers set the random forest (`r round(res_rf$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)`, R²
`r round(res_rf$drivers$best$cv_r2, 2)`) clearly beats every linear model. The grid surface is fairly flat, so the
forest isn't sensitive to its exact settings, which is typical. Adding the district barely helps the forest
(`r round(res_rf$district$best$cv_rmse, 4)`), and in that set it falls behind the linear models. Trees handle a
65-level category poorly: the district information gets spread across many small, noisy splits. A linear model
gives each district its own intercept directly.

# XGBoost (gradient-boosted trees)

**What it is.** Small trees are built one after another, each fitted to the errors left by the previous ones, and
only a fraction `eta` (the learning rate) of each is added. A forest averages independent trees; boosting adds
dependent ones.

**Tuned:**

* `max_depth`: how many splits deep each tree may go (its order of interactions).
* `min_child_weight`: the minimum size of a leaf.
* `nrounds`: how many trees. Too few under-fits; too many over-fits. As with λ for the lasso, one fit of 3,000
  rounds lets us score every round count from 25 to 3,000 at no extra cost. The range goes up to 3,000 so that the
  chosen number of rounds is not at the edge of what we tried.

Fixed:

* `eta` = 0.03 (a slow, safe learning rate);
* `subsample` = `colsample_bytree` = 0.8 (each tree sees 80% of rows and features, which adds randomness like a
  forest).

```{r xgb, cache = TRUE}
xgb_checkpoints <- seq(25, 3000, by = 25)

fp_xgb <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p) {
  rhs <- rhs_of(vars)
  set.seed(462)
  booster <- xgb.train(
    params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.03,
                  max_depth = p$max_depth, min_child_weight = p$min_child_weight,
                  subsample = 0.8, colsample_bytree = 0.8, nthread = N_CORES),
    data = xgb.DMatrix(make_x(tr, rhs), label = tr[[y]]),
    nrounds = max(xgb_checkpoints), verbose = 0)
  new_x <- xgb.DMatrix(make_x(nw, rhs))
  pred  <- sapply(xgb_checkpoints, \(k) predict(booster, new_x, iterationrange = c(1, k)))
  colnames(pred) <- xgb_checkpoints
  pred
}
res_xgb <- tune_model(fp_xgb, grid = expand_grid(max_depth = c(2, 4, 6, 8), min_child_weight = c(1, 10)),
                      inner = "nrounds")
summarise_tuning(res_xgb, "XGBoost") |> select(set, best_settings, cv_rmse, cv_r2, seconds) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

```{r xgb-curve, fig.height = 3.6}
xgb_curve <- res_xgb$drivers$summary |>
  mutate(setting = paste0("depth ", max_depth, ", min_child_weight ", min_child_weight))
p_xgb <- ggplot(xgb_curve, aes(nrounds, cv_rmse, colour = setting)) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(min(xgb_curve$cv_rmse) - 0.001, min(xgb_curve$cv_rmse) + 0.01)) +
  labs(title = "XGBoost (drivers set): CV error as trees are added",
       subtitle = "Error falls, flattens, then creeps up as later trees start fitting noise",
       x = "Number of boosting rounds (trees)", y = "CV RMSE (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
save_fig(p_xgb, "fig18_xgb_rounds", height = 3.6, width = 8)
```

**Observation.** The curves show the bias–variance trade-off:

* Deeper trees reach their best after a few hundred rounds and then get worse (over-fitting).
* Depth-2 trees learn slowly and keep improving for longer.
* The best settings sit in a broad, flat valley, so the exact choice matters little.

On the drivers set XGBoost (`r round(res_xgb$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)`) is level with the random forest. On the
district set it prefers very shallow trees (depth `r res_xgb$district$best$max_depth`, `r res_xgb$district$best$nrounds`
rounds). Shallow trees add up to something close to an additive model, which is what the linear models are telling us
too.

# Support vector machine (SVM) regression

**What it is.** With a radial kernel, the SVM predicts each row mainly from the training rows closest to it in
feature space. Errors smaller than ε are ignored and larger ones are penalised with weight `cost`. Features are
standardised first (`scale = TRUE`), because distances are meaningless when features have different units.

**Tuned:**

* `gamma` (γ): how local the influence of each training row is. A large γ gives a very wiggly fit.
* `cost`: how hard the model tries to fit every point. A large cost gives less smoothing.

ε is fixed at 0.05 (≈ 5% on the log scale).

```{r svm, cache = TRUE}
fp_svm <- function(vars, y) function(tr, nw, p) {
  rhs <- rhs_of(vars)
  fit <- svm(make_x(tr, rhs), tr[[y]], type = "eps-regression", kernel = "radial",
             cost = p$cost, gamma = p$gamma, epsilon = 0.05, scale = TRUE)
  as.numeric(predict(fit, make_x(nw, rhs)))
}
res_svm <- tune_model(fp_svm, grid = expand_grid(cost = c(0.3, 1, 3), gamma = c(0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1)))
summarise_tuning(res_svm, "SVM (radial)") |> select(set, best_settings, cv_rmse, cv_r2, seconds) |> kable(digits = 4)
```

**Observation.** The SVM is best or joint-best on the drivers set (`r round(res_svm$drivers$best$cv_rmse, 4)`) and
close to the best on the district set (`r round(res_svm$district$best$cv_rmse, 4)`). It is the slowest to tune
(`r round(attr(res_svm$district, "seconds"))` s for the district set). Its predictions can't be broken down by
feature, so it is the hardest of the models to explain. The district set prefers a small γ, i.e. a smooth,
nearly linear surface, again pointing to mostly additive effects once location is known.

# Cross-validation comparison of all models

```{r cv-table}
model_order <- c("Overall mean", "District mean", "Linear regression", "Polynomial regression", "Ridge",
                 "Elastic net", "Lasso", "GAM (splines)", "Regression tree", "Random forest", "XGBoost",
                 "SVM (radial)")

# every model's tuning result, its factory, and its inner setting (if any)
spec <- list(
  "Overall mean"          = list(res = res_mean,     fp = fp_mean),
  "District mean"         = list(res = res_distmean, fp = fp_district_mean),
  "Linear regression"     = list(res = res_ols,      fp = fp_ols),
  "Polynomial regression" = list(res = res_poly,     fp = fp_poly),
  "Ridge"                 = list(res = res_ridge,    fp = fp_glmnet, inner = "lambda"),
  "Elastic net"           = list(res = res_enet,     fp = fp_glmnet, inner = "lambda"),
  "Lasso"                 = list(res = res_lasso,    fp = fp_glmnet, inner = "lambda"),
  "GAM (splines)"         = list(res = res_gam,      fp = fp_gam),
  "Regression tree"       = list(res = res_tree,     fp = fp_tree),
  "Random forest"         = list(res = res_rf,       fp = fp_rf),
  "XGBoost"               = list(res = res_xgb,      fp = fp_xgb, inner = "nrounds"),
  "SVM (radial)"          = list(res = res_svm,      fp = fp_svm)
)

cv_all <- imap_dfr(spec, \(s, m) summarise_tuning(s$res, m)) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = model_order),
         set = factor(set, levels = c("none", "drivers", "district"))) |>
  arrange(set, model)
cvv <- function(m, s, col = "cv_rmse") cv_all[[col]][cv_all$model == m & cv_all$set == s]   # for inline text
# later cached chunks (test, importance, real response) also depend on the tuning results
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache.extra = list(file_md5, rlang::hash(list(train, test, folds, fsets, Y, cv_all))))
save_tab(cv_all, "t08_cv_results") |>
  select(set, model, best_settings, cv_rmse, cv_rmse_se, cv_mae, cv_r2, seconds) |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Cross-validation results (training years only), best setting of each model")
```

```{r cv-plot, fig.height = 4.6}
cv_plot_df <- bind_rows(
  cv_all |> filter(set != "none"),
  cv_all |> filter(set == "none") |> mutate(set = "drivers"),
  cv_all |> filter(set == "none") |> mutate(set = "district")) |>
  mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("drivers", "district"),
                      labels = c("Drivers only", "Drivers + district")))

p_cv <- ggplot(cv_plot_df, aes(cv_rmse, fct_rev(model))) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = cv_rmse - cv_rmse_se, xmax = cv_rmse + cv_rmse_se), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = model %in% c("Overall mean", "District mean")), size = 2.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(data = cv_plot_df |> filter(model == "District mean"), aes(xintercept = cv_rmse),
             linetype = 2, colour = "#e76f51") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#e76f51", `FALSE` = "#2a6f97")) +
  facet_wrap(~set) +
  labs(title = "Cross-validated error of every model (lower is better)",
       subtitle = "Point = mean over 4 time-ordered folds; bar = ±1 standard error; dashed = district-mean baseline",
       x = "CV RMSE (log scale, ≈ proportional error)", y = NULL)
save_fig(p_cv, "fig19_cv_comparison", height = 4.6, width = 8)
```

```{r one-se}
one_se <- cv_all |>
  filter(set != "none") |>
  group_by(set) |>
  mutate(best_rmse = min(cv_rmse),
         threshold = best_rmse + cv_rmse_se[which.min(cv_rmse)],
         within_1se = cv_rmse <= threshold) |>
  ungroup()

chosen <- one_se |> filter(within_1se) |> group_by(set) |> arrange(model) |> slice(1) |> ungroup()
one_se |> filter(within_1se) |> select(set, model, cv_rmse, threshold) |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Models within one standard error of the best (listed simplest first)")
chosen |> select(set, model, best_settings, cv_rmse)  |> kable(digits = 4, caption = "Chosen by the 1-SE rule")
```

**Observation.** Three findings.

1. **Drivers only.** The flexible models form the top group:
   * random forest `r round(cvv("Random forest", "drivers"), 4)`;
   * XGBoost `r round(cvv("XGBoost", "drivers"), 4)`;
   * SVM `r round(cvv("SVM (radial)", "drivers"), 4)`.

   They are ahead of the whole linear family (`r round(cvv("Polynomial regression", "drivers"), 4)`–`r round(cvv("Linear regression", "drivers"), 4)`).
   They explain about a third of the variation in relative cost (CV R² ≈ `r round(cvv("SVM (radial)", "drivers", "cv_r2"), 2)`),
   versus about a quarter for the linear models. The measured drivers matter in a non-linear, interacting way.
   **But no drivers-only model clearly beats the district-mean baseline** (`r round(cvv("District mean", "none"), 4)`).
   Our measured features recover about as much as simply knowing the district, and no more.
2. **Drivers + district.** Here the order flips: the **linear models are best**
   (lasso `r round(cvv("Lasso", "district"), 4)`, plain linear regression `r round(cvv("Linear regression", "district"), 4)`,
   R² about `r round(cvv("Linear regression", "district", "cv_r2"), 2)`). XGBoost and the SVM are level with them, while
   forests and single trees fall behind. Once each district has its own level, what is left is mostly additive and close to linear.
   These models beat the district-mean baseline by about
   `r fmt_pct(1 - cvv("Lasso", "district") / cvv("District mean", "none"), 0)` in RMSE. The drivers explain movements
   *around* each district's usual level.
3. **The 1-SE rule** picks **`r chosen$model[chosen$set == "drivers"]`** for the drivers set and
   **`r chosen$model[chosen$set == "district"]`** for the district set. These are the models we carry forward, but
   we still report every model on the test set.

# Final evaluation on the test years (2020–2026)

Each model is refitted at its tuned settings on **all** 1996–2019 training rows, then scored once on the 1,600 test
rows.

```{r test-eval, cache = TRUE}
test_pred <- imap_dfr(spec, function(s, m) {
  sets <- if (m %in% c("Overall mean", "District mean")) list(none = character(0)) else fsets
  preds <- refit_predict(s$fp, s$res, sets, Y, train, test, inner = s$inner)
  imap_dfr(preds, \(p, set) tibble(model = m, set = set, row = seq_along(p), pred = p))
})
```

```{r test-table}
test_long <- test_pred |>
  left_join(test |> mutate(row = row_number()) |>
              select(row, ta, yq, year, obs = all_of(Y), loo_cost_m2, real_cost_m2), by = "row") |>
  mutate(pred_dollars = exp(pred) * loo_cost_m2)

test_res <- test_long |>
  group_by(model, set) |>
  summarise(reg_metrics(obs, pred), mape = mape(real_cost_m2, pred_dollars), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(cv_all |> select(model, set, cv_rmse), by = c("model", "set")) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = model_order),
         set = factor(set, levels = c("none", "drivers", "district"))) |>
  arrange(set, model) |>
  rename(test_rmse = rmse, test_mae = mae, test_r2 = r2, test_mape = mape)
tv <- function(m, s, col = "test_rmse") test_res[[col]][test_res$model == m & test_res$set == s]   # for inline text
save_tab(test_res, "t09_test_results") |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Test-period scores (2020Q1–2026Q2). MAPE is on real $/m².")
```

```{r cv-vs-test, fig.height = 4.6}
cvtest_df <- bind_rows(
  test_res |> filter(set != "none"),
  test_res |> filter(set == "none") |> mutate(set = "drivers"),
  test_res |> filter(set == "none") |> mutate(set = "district")) |>
  mutate(set = factor(as.character(set), levels = c("drivers", "district"),
                      labels = c("Drivers only", "Drivers + district"))) |>
  pivot_longer(c(cv_rmse, test_rmse), names_to = "score", values_to = "rmse") |>
  mutate(score = recode(score, cv_rmse = "CV (1996–2019)", test_rmse = "Test (2020–2026)"))

p_cvtest <- ggplot(cvtest_df, aes(rmse, fct_rev(model))) +
  geom_line(aes(group = model), colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = score), size = 2.3) +
  geom_vline(data = cvtest_df |> filter(model == "District mean", score == "Test (2020–2026)"),
             aes(xintercept = rmse), linetype = 2, colour = "#e76f51") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("CV (1996–2019)" = "grey55", "Test (2020–2026)" = "#2a6f97")) +
  facet_wrap(~set) +
  labs(title = "Cross-validation vs test error for every model",
       subtitle = "Dashed = district-mean baseline on the test years. Every model is worse after 2020.",
       x = "RMSE (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
save_fig(p_cvtest, "fig20_cv_vs_test", height = 4.6, width = 8)
```

```{r pred-vs-actual, fig.height = 4}
chosen_pred <- test_long |> semi_join(chosen |> mutate(model = as.character(model), set = as.character(set)),
                                      by = c("model", "set")) |>
  mutate(panel = paste0(model, " (", set, " set)"))
p_pva <- ggplot(chosen_pred, aes(pred, obs)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50", linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1, colour = "#2a6f97") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#e76f51", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  labs(title = "Chosen models on the test years: predicted vs actual relative cost",
       x = "Predicted (log ratio to rest of NZ)", y = "Actual")
save_fig(p_pva, "fig21_test_pred_vs_actual", height = 4, width = 8)
```

**Observation.** Five points.

1. **Every model is worse on 2020–26 than in CV, including the overall mean**
   (`r round(tv("Overall mean", "none"), 3)` vs `r round(cvv("Overall mean", "none"), 3)`). So part of this is not the
   models' fault: districts were simply *more spread out* relative to each other in the COVID / boom / bust years.
   R² adjusts for this, and the R² values are close to the CV ones.
2. **The district set beats the drivers set again.** The best district-set model reaches test RMSE
   `r round(min(test_res$test_rmse[test_res$set == "district"]), 4)` (R²
   ≈ `r round(max(test_res$test_r2[test_res$set == "district"]), 2)`). The best drivers-only model reaches
   `r round(min(test_res$test_rmse[test_res$set == "drivers"]), 4)` (R²
   ≈ `r round(max(test_res$test_r2[test_res$set == "drivers"]), 2)`).
3. **The district-mean baseline is hard to beat out of sample.** It scores `r round(tv("District mean", "none"), 4)`
   (MAPE `r fmt_pct(tv("District mean", "none", "test_mape"), 1)`). The best models improve on it only marginally. In
   predictive terms, *where* a house is built tells you most of what our features can tell you.
4. **Chosen models:**
   * **`r chosen$model[chosen$set == "drivers"]`, drivers:** test RMSE
     `r round(tv(as.character(chosen$model[chosen$set == "drivers"]), "drivers"), 4)`, MAPE
     `r fmt_pct(tv(as.character(chosen$model[chosen$set == "drivers"]), "drivers", "test_mape"), 1)`;
   * **`r chosen$model[chosen$set == "district"]`, district:** test RMSE
     `r round(tv(as.character(chosen$model[chosen$set == "district"]), "district"), 4)`, MAPE
     `r fmt_pct(tv(as.character(chosen$model[chosen$set == "district"]), "district", "test_mape"), 1)`.

   A typical district-quarter is predicted within about 8% of its actual $/m².
5. **The CV ranking mostly held:** flexible models led on drivers only, and linear models were competitive with
   district. The order *within* each top group shuffled, which is what you expect when differences are inside one
   standard error.

In the predicted-vs-actual plot, the fitted (orange) line is **steeper than 45° and sits slightly above it**.
Steeper means the actual relative costs in 2020–26 were *more spread out* than the models predicted. The models are
conservative: dear districts turned out even dearer and cheap ones even cheaper. Above means the average relative
cost rose a little (Step 2: −0.04 → −0.01), which a model trained on 1996–2019 can't know. Both match point 1.

# What drives relative cost? (variable importance)

We use the **drivers** set here. In the district set, the district name absorbs most of the location effect and
hides which measurable features matter. Three views from three different model types:

* **Lasso, standardised coefficients:** the size of each coefficient after features are put on the same scale
  (1 SD). The sign gives the direction.
* **Random forest, permutation importance:** how much the forest's out-of-bag error rises when one feature's values
  are shuffled (breaking its link to the response).
* **XGBoost, gain:** the share of total error reduction contributed by splits on each feature.

Dummy columns (regions) are added back together into one `region` score.

```{r importance, cache = TRUE}
vars <- fsets$drivers; rhs <- rhs_of(vars)
x_tr <- make_x(train, rhs)
base_var <- function(col) map_chr(col, \(cn) vars[which(startsWith(cn, vars))[1]])

# lasso at the CV-chosen lambda, coefficients x feature SD = standardised effect
lasso_fit <- glmnet(x_tr, train[[Y]], alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_grid)
b <- as.matrix(coef(lasso_fit, s = res_lasso$drivers$best$lambda))[-1, 1]
imp_lasso <- tibble(column = names(b), value = b * apply(x_tr, 2, sd)) |>
  mutate(feature = base_var(column)) |>
  group_by(feature) |> summarise(signed = value[which.max(abs(value))], importance = sum(abs(value)))

# random forest permutation importance at the tuned settings
bt <- res_rf$drivers$best
rf_fit <- ranger(fml_of(Y, vars), data = train, num.trees = 500, mtry = bt$mtry,
                 min.node.size = bt$min.node.size, importance = "permutation",
                 num.threads = N_CORES, seed = 462)
imp_rf <- tibble(feature = names(rf_fit$variable.importance), importance = rf_fit$variable.importance)

# xgboost gain at the tuned settings
bx <- res_xgb$drivers$best
set.seed(462)
xgb_fit <- xgb.train(params = list(objective = "reg:squarederror", eta = 0.03, max_depth = bx$max_depth,
                                   min_child_weight = bx$min_child_weight, subsample = 0.8,
                                   colsample_bytree = 0.8, nthread = N_CORES),
                     data = xgb.DMatrix(x_tr, label = train[[Y]]), nrounds = bx$nrounds, verbose = 0)
imp_xgb <- xgb.importance(model = xgb_fit) |> as_tibble() |>
  mutate(feature = base_var(Feature)) |> group_by(feature) |> summarise(importance = sum(Gain))

importance <- bind_rows(
  imp_lasso |> transmute(feature, method = "Lasso |std. coef|", importance, direction = sign(signed)),
  imp_rf    |> transmute(feature, method = "Random forest permutation", importance),
  imp_xgb   |> transmute(feature, method = "XGBoost gain", importance)) |>
  group_by(method) |> mutate(share = importance / sum(importance)) |> ungroup()
```

```{r importance-plot, fig.height = 4.8}
imp_order <- importance |> group_by(feature) |> summarise(m = mean(share)) |> arrange(m) |> pull(feature)
lasso_sign <- importance |> filter(method == "Lasso |std. coef|") |> select(feature, direction)

p_imp <- importance |>
  left_join(lasso_sign, by = "feature", suffix = c("", "_lasso")) |>
  mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = imp_order),
         dir = case_when(feature %in% c("region") ~ "category",
                         direction_lasso > 0 ~ "dearer when higher",
                         direction_lasso < 0 ~ "cheaper when higher",
                         TRUE ~ "dropped by lasso")) |>
  ggplot(aes(share, feature, fill = dir)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~method) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`dearer when higher` = "#e76f51", `cheaper when higher` = "#2a6f97",
                               category = "grey60", `dropped by lasso` = "grey85")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "What drives a district's relative cost per m²? (drivers set, training years)",
       subtitle = "Share of each model's total importance; colour = direction in the lasso",
       x = "Share of importance", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
save_fig(p_imp, "fig22_variable_importance", height = 4.8, width = 9)

importance |> select(feature, method, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = share) |>
  arrange(desc(`Random forest permutation`)) |>
  save_tab("t10_variable_importance") |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Share of importance by method")
```

**Observation.** The three methods work in quite different ways, yet they agree on the top four:

1. **Residential alteration spending** (`log_resid_alt_real`, dearer when higher) is the top numeric driver in all
   three. Districts where people spend a lot renovating are wealthier, with dearer land, higher specifications and
   busier trades.
2. **Region** (a category; the lasso share adds up 15 dummy coefficients, which inflates it): broad location still
   matters after the other features.
3. **New dwellings per 1,000 residents** (dearer when higher): fast-growing places, where builders are stretched.
4. **Number of new houses** (`log_houses_n`, **cheaper** when higher, holding the others fixed). For a given level of
   wealth and growth, districts building *many* houses are cheaper per m². This is consistent with volume builders
   and large greenfield subdivisions such as Selwyn.

Next come **relative house size** (bigger houses are cheaper per m², because fixed costs such as kitchens and
bathrooms are spread over more floor area), then non-residential activity and growth. The dwelling-mix shares
(apartments, townhouses, retirement) matter little.

Remember these are *associations* in observational data. For example, more alteration spending in a district does
not *cause* dearer new houses; both reflect a wealthier, busier building market. Step 4 will look at *how* each
top driver changes predictions (partial dependence) and at which districts the model gets wrong.

# Secondary response: log real $/m² and the extrapolation problem

The pitch's original target was real $/m² itself. Here we add the national time trend `t_index` and use
`avg_house_m2` (absolute size), and fit a subset of the models on the same folds.

```{r real-response, cache = TRUE}
Y2 <- "log_real_cost_m2"
num_real <- c("avg_house_m2", setdiff(num_main, "rel_house_m2"), "t_index")
fsets_real <- list(drivers = c(num_real, "region", "is_city"), district = c(num_real, "ta"))

real_spec <- list(
  "District mean"     = list(fp = fp_district_mean, sets = list(none = character(0))),
  "Linear regression" = list(fp = fp_ols),
  "Lasso"             = list(fp = fp_glmnet, grid = tibble(alpha = 1), inner = "lambda"),
  "Regression tree"   = list(fp = fp_tree, grid = expand_grid(cp = c(0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01), minbucket = c(10, 30))),
  "Random forest"     = list(fp = fp_rf, grid = expand_grid(mtry = c(4, 8), min.node.size = c(5, 20))),
  "XGBoost"           = list(fp = fp_xgb, grid = expand_grid(max_depth = c(4, 6), min_child_weight = c(1, 10)),
                             inner = "nrounds")
)
real_res <- imap(real_spec, function(s, m) {
  sets <- s$sets %||% fsets_real
  r    <- tune_model(s$fp, grid = s$grid, inner = s$inner, sets = sets, y = Y2)
  p    <- refit_predict(s$fp, r, sets, Y2, train, test, inner = s$inner)
  list(res = r, pred = p)
})
```

```{r real-results}
real_test <- imap_dfr(real_res, function(x, m) imap_dfr(x$pred, \(p, set)
  tibble(model = m, set = set, row = seq_along(p), pred = p))) |>
  left_join(test |> mutate(row = row_number()) |> select(row, yq, year, obs = log_real_cost_m2, real_cost_m2),
            by = "row")

real_table <- real_test |>
  group_by(model, set) |>
  summarise(reg_metrics(obs, pred), mape = mape(real_cost_m2, exp(pred)),
            mean_bias = mean(pred - obs), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(imap_dfr(real_res, \(x, m) summarise_tuning(x$res, m)) |> select(model, set, cv_rmse),
            by = c("model", "set")) |>
  rename(test_rmse = rmse, test_mae = mae, test_r2 = r2, test_mape = mape) |>
  arrange(set, test_rmse)
save_tab(real_table, "t11_real_response_results") |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Log real $/m² (with time trend): CV and test scores. mean_bias < 0 = under-predicts.")
```

```{r real-plot, fig.height = 4.2}
real_nat <- real_test |>
  filter(set %in% c("district", "none")) |>
  group_by(model, yq, year) |>
  summarise(pred = exp(mean(pred)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(t = as.numeric(substr(yq, 1, 4)) + (as.numeric(substr(yq, 6, 6)) - 1) / 4)
actual_nat <- dat |> filter(year >= 2010) |> group_by(yq) |>
  summarise(actual = exp(mean(log_real_cost_m2)), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(t = as.numeric(substr(yq, 1, 4)) + (as.numeric(substr(yq, 6, 6)) - 1) / 4)

p_real <- ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = actual_nat, aes(t, actual), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(data = real_nat, aes(t, pred, colour = model), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2020, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 2020.1, y = max(actual_nat$actual), label = "test period →", hjust = 0, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Real $/m² after 2019: trees flatten out, straight-line trends overshoot",
       subtitle = "Black = actual (geometric mean across districts); colours = test predictions, district set",
       x = NULL, y = "Real $/m² (June 2026 $)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
save_fig(p_real, "fig23_real_cost_extrapolation", height = 4.2, width = 8)
```

**Observation.** Each model family fails in its own characteristic way once it has to predict a *level* it never
saw:

* **District mean:** ignores time entirely and under-predicts by about
  `r fmt_pct(-real_table$mean_bias[real_table$model == "District mean"], 0)`.
* **Regression tree and random forest:** predictions flatten at roughly the last level in the training data and
  stay there (mean bias `r round(real_table$mean_bias[real_table$model == "Regression tree" & real_table$set == "district"], 3)`
  and `r round(real_table$mean_bias[real_table$model == "Random forest" & real_table$set == "district"], 3)`). A
  tree can only output averages of training rows, so `t_index` beyond 2019 is treated like 2019.
* **Linear and lasso:** they carry the 1996–2019 trend forward as a straight line and **overshoot** (mean bias
  `r sprintf("%+.3f", real_table$mean_bias[real_table$model == "Linear regression" & real_table$set == "district"])`),
  because real costs after 2019 rose more slowly than the 1996–2019 trend.
* **XGBoost** happens to land closest. It leans on activity features (alterations, growth) that *did* move in the
  test years, rather than on the clock. That is a lucky proxy, not a reliable mechanism.

This is why the **relative** response is the main one for RQ1. It removes the national level, so no model has to
guess the future price level, and it asks a question that the pre-2020 data can answer.

# Summary and next step

```{r save-results}
saveRDS(list(cv = cv_all, test = test_res, chosen = chosen, importance = importance,
             real = real_table, test_predictions = test_long,
             best_settings = map(spec, \(s) map(s$res, "best"))),
        file.path(paths$models_rq1, "rq1_step3_results.rds"))
list.files(paths$models_rq1)
```

| # | Finding | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | With drivers only, the flexible models (forest, XGBoost, SVM) beat the linear family: CV R² ≈ 0.32 vs 0.23–0.25. | The drivers act non-linearly and in combination. |
| 2 | No drivers-only model clearly beats "each district's own average" (CV or test). | Our measured features capture roughly what location captures, not more. Part of the location effect remains unexplained (land, terrain, local costs). |
| 3 | With the district added, linear models are best (CV R² ≈ 0.38–0.39), and they beat the district mean. The penalty adds little, so the 1-SE rule keeps plain linear regression. | The drivers explain movements around each district's usual level, and mostly additively. |
| 4 | Main drivers: alteration spending (+), region, dwellings per 1,000 residents (+), number of new houses (−), house size (−). | This is the answer to "what drives" for the report. Step 4 will show the shapes. |
| 5 | Every model is worse in 2020–26, the baseline included. | The test years were unusually dispersed (COVID, boom, bust). The ranking mostly held. |
| 6 | On real $/m², trees flatten and linear trends overshoot. | Confirms the relative response as the main RQ1 target. |

**Step 4 (next):**

* interpret the chosen models (partial-dependence plots for the top drivers);
* look at test errors by district and year (where is the model wrong?);
* optionally refine the tuning grid around the winner;
* write the RQ1 answer for the report.
